title: NPS for NRIs: What You Need to Know About Tax Savings, Withdrawals and Repatriation Rules
excerpt: India's National Pension System remains one of the few retirement instruments NRIs can access, but the tax and repatriation rules are more complex than many realise.
body:
• NRIs aged 18-70 can open and contribute to NPS accounts in India, with investments denominated in Indian Rupees.
  • Tax deductions of up to Rs 2 lakh are available under the old regime (Rs 1.5 lakh under 80CCD(1) plus Rs 50,000 under 80CCD(1B)), but only for NRIs filing returns in India.
  • At maturity, 60% of the corpus can be withdrawn tax-free; the remaining 40% must be used to purchase an annuity taxed at slab rates.
  • Repatriation is permitted under FEMA rules — freely for NRE-funded accounts, up to $1 million annually for NRO-funded accounts.

India's National Pension System remains one of the most accessible retirement savings instruments for Non-Resident Indians, offering tax-advantaged returns in a country where many alternative products — like the Public Provident Fund — are closed to new NRI accounts. But the eligibility criteria, tax implications and repatriation rules carry nuances that can catch the uninformed off guard.

Who Can Invest

NRIs and Overseas Citizens of India (OCIs) aged 18 to 70 can open NPS accounts through the eNPS portal using their PAN, Aadhaar and a registered mobile number. Hindu Undivided Families are not eligible. Contributions must be made through NRE or NRO bank accounts in Indian Rupees, with a minimum annual contribution of Rs 1,000 to keep the account active, according to Livemint.

The scheme offers two tiers: Tier I (mandatory, with tax benefits and lock-in until age 60) and Tier II (optional, for flexible savings without tax advantages). Subscribers can choose their asset allocation across equity, corporate bonds and government securities, or opt for the age-based Auto Choice mode.

Tax Benefits: Old vs New Regime

Under the old tax regime, NRIs filing Indian tax returns can claim deductions of up to Rs 1.5 lakh under Section 80CCD(1) and an additional Rs 50,000 under Section 80CCD(1B) — a total tax benefit of up to Rs 2 lakh annually. However, under the new regime, only employer contributions qualify for deductions, which does not apply to most NRIs.

"These benefits are only available if you're filing returns in India," tax expert Shah told Livemint. Returns on the NPS account are not taxed in India until withdrawal, but they may be taxed in the subscriber's country of residence.

"Even if your account is temporarily frozen due to non-payment of the minimum contribution, investment returns will continue to accrue."

— Shah, NPS tax expert, quoted by Livemint

Withdrawal and Exit Rules

At maturity (age 60), subscribers can withdraw up to 60% of the corpus tax-free under Section 10(12A). The remaining 40% must be used to purchase an annuity, with the annuity income taxed at applicable slab rates. For premature exits, at least 80% must go toward an annuity, with only 20% available as a lump sum.

Partial withdrawals of up to 25% of self-contributions are permitted after three years, subject to specific conditions such as children's education, home purchase or medical emergencies.

Repatriation: NRE vs NRO

The accumulated NPS corpus is repatriable under FEMA regulations, but the channel matters. Funds invested through NRE accounts are freely repatriable, while NRO-funded accounts face a $1 million annual limit with required documentation including Form 15CB from a Chartered Accountant. Annuity payouts are credited to the subscriber's NRO account and can be remitted overseas subject to RBI limits.

NPS returns have historically ranged between 8-12% depending on the asset mix, making it competitive with mutual funds while offering the security of a regulated pension framework. For NRIs planning eventual retirement in India, the rupee-denominated investment also reduces currency conversion risk at the withdrawal stage.
nri_angle: NPS remains one of the few retirement instruments available to NRIs, offering tax-advantaged returns and repatriable corpus under FEMA rules.
